item.title: Data Platforms Are Becoming a Supervision Problem
item.dc:creator: Abhilash Rao Mesala
item.description: The real data engineering problem of the next few years is to make our verification systems smart enough to give us confidence that agent-authored changes are semantically correct.
item.content:encoded:
I opened a pull request (PR) one day that changed an integer column to a big integer and updated a transformation. All of the tests passed. They should not have.

Two steps upstream, an agent had earlier changed how we handled nulls, and that change was the reason my tests were green. It didn’t trip any of our existing sanity checks, because those checks had been passing for years and nobody had looked hard at what they actually asserted. What we had assumed for years was that a null in that column meant “not yet measured.” After the agent’s change, those same rows would read as zeros. The pipeline was green, and it was quietly wrong.

This is one of those moments where a client sends you a confused email and you go back to the code repository for the twentieth time. What’s going on here? You check the test coverage, and it all looks good. You sit with your mental model of how the transformation works and what it does, and it all makes sense. But something is off. It turns out that agent-authored data work has turned verification into a supervision problem, and the way we have been reviewing this work doesn’t help in any meaningful way.

Supervising agent-authored data is harder than reviewing agent-authored code, because software has a much stronger contract. A piece of software passing tests maps strongly to the intended behavior being tested, because that behavior is usually written directly in the code. In data work, the critical meaning lives somewhere else: in the distribution of the data, its history, and context, and a pile of assumptions that live in some code but are rarely encoded anywhere specific. Local validity can produce global error. Schemas and backfills can be “cleanly wrong.”

One example makes the shape of it clear. Agent A fixes a query bug by changing the join semantics (the rules that decide which rows from two tables get matched and combined), and reports that this resolves a downstream discrepancy. The change survives every test and passes code review, because nothing in the tests encodes the assumption it violated. Weeks later, agent B runs a backfill in a downstream pipeline against that same, now subtly different, upstream table. Only then does someone notice that a revenue number has been inflated the entire time. Both changes were clean; neither was correct.

This is the failure mode that matters most. Pipelines rarely crash under agents. They keep running. The errors they produce tend to be subtle, plausible, and quiet, and quiet errors are decision-level risks.

We need to build a supervision layer to handle this, because the old way of doing reviews is not sufficient. So what should supervision check, if telling someone to “review the change carefully” doesn’t scale?

I put the question on a notepad and jotted down a few buckets of things to check.

Bucket 1: Compare the Effect, Not the Text

The first idea was to compare what a change would do, rather than what text was changed. This is where the most bang for the buck is, and it comes down to a few key features. Does the change affect the overall row count in this dimension? Does it change the null rate of the asset we derive from it? Is there an obvious shift in the distribution of values before and after a run? Does the value of a particular metric move after the change is applied?

None of this is about what’s in the code change. It’s about inferring what the change would do to the data it’s applied to.

Bucket 2: Make Assumptions Checkable

The second bucket was contracts made explicit. I expect the older data platform era to give way to one where agents write transformation code and lean heavily on producer-side schemas. The more agents touch producer-side data, the more they will need a full data contract, and the less appropriate it becomes to treat contracts as negotiable and opt-in. They are too central to be optional.

We should move whatever assumptions we can from the tacit category of “unwritten expectations” into the explicit category of “expectations we can assert programmatically about a dataset.” The classic example is that a null in this field implies a value in that field. Data contracts make this kind of thing far less error-prone by forcing it into the open.

Bucket 3: Reduce Blast Radius with Lineage

If your job is to verify what will happen when a code change alters the data, then you need to know every consumer of that change. Lineage is what tells you the blast radius. It is the difference between an edit that looks risky but does nothing harmful, and an edit that is a silent break to everything flowing downstream of a transformation.

This is where lineage tools such as OpenLineage fit as a feature of supervision, alongside data verification and testing systems such as dbt tests and Great Expectations as cues for where impact could land. These are existing pieces of the ecosystem. My near-term expectation is that this will be less about inventing new technology and more about redirecting the tools we already have at the output of agents.

Organizational Counterpoint: Supervision Is Currently Nobody’s Job

These technical gaps sit inside an ownership gap, and that is the part I find more uncomfortable than the technical one. Code review has an owner: one person assigned a ticket and responsible for signing off. On-call has a rotation, shared across the team. Supervision of agent-authored data transformations tends to be the responsibility of whoever happens to be working on data that day.

That was fine when an agent opened maybe one PR of work a week. There was enough time to look through the work in progress, check a few columns, run tests, maybe run a downstream observation or two. But now agents open twenty PRs of work, with downstreams of both direct and indirect impact, where a wrong number at an upstream step can send a downstream system off on a long, incorrect investigation or a bad decision. Opportunistic checking, done when someone has time, turns into a lost opportunity and a real risk that work ships unverified simply because no one noticed the change.

What Not to Do, and What Tests Must Become

Finally, what not to do. I would not slow the agents down by forcing them into back-and-forth with humans for feedback. Agents make the platform faster, and in the new status quo, the data they produce is often better than what came before, so slowing them down is a bad trade.

But that points straight at the obvious counterproposal: If you shouldn’t slow the agents down, just make the supervision system faster. That is probably what I would recommend too, but only after working through the ownership gap above.

The deeper issue is what we now mean by “green tests.” When humans wrote the changes, tests confirmed that work we mostly trusted was behaving correctly. When agents write the changes, tests become the main barrier standing between that work and production. In a supervised world, tests need to fail on things that are genuinely bad to have in the system, and black-box tests won’t tell us as much as checking contracts across the data path, checking data quality downstream, and checking lineage and blast radius.

So the synthesis is a clear focus on closing the gap between tests and supervision, so that silent semantic failures get caught before they ruin a downstream decision.

My central thesis is this: pipelines authored by agents demand that we staff and engineer a real supervision layer for data changes, the same way we built real testing and real observability layers before it. That layer should rest on a fairly obvious insight, one that is especially reachable now that data contracts are in scope at many companies: the hardest part of semantic correctness in data platforms is not reading the code changes line by line. It is surfacing the semantic differences between changes in production pipelines, and ensuring that changes obey their contracts at every level of the data value chain. The real data engineering problem of the next few years is to make our verification systems smart enough to give us confidence that agent-authored changes are semantically correct and contract-obeying.

Disclosure: I used LLMs to help organize and shape the draft. The ideas, technical details, and analysis are based on my own work, and I have reviewed the final text and agree with it.

Abhilash Rao Mesala is a Data & AI Leader, where he works on large-scale data infrastructure that powers business-critical analytics. Over roughly 14 years he has led data platform and pipeline initiatives across enterprise environments, with a focus on scalable architecture and high-stakes production data systems. He writes at the intersection of data engineering and the operational complexity of systems that organizations depend on to make consequential decisions.

item.title: Ensuring Epistemic Security in AI-Driven Cyber Investigations
item.dc:creator: Eoghan Casey
item.description: There is a pressing need for systematic and efficient approaches to codifying and reusing existing cyber investigation expertise to ensure accurate and reliable forensic findings.
item.content:encoded:
Cyber investigators face growing challenges, including big data, technological advances, and concealment activities. Computing is evolving rapidly and digital evidence is increasing in volume, velocity, variety, and complexity, making it difficult for one person to keep up and have full knowledge in all areas. Rising backlogs are causing justice to be delayed, or even denied, when a cyber investigation cannot be completed in a timely manner. Increasingly, criminals and artificial intelligence (AI) agents are employing a variety of tampering methods that make it more difficult to find digital traces of their activities. Relevant information is being overlooked and misinterpreted, missing investigative opportunities and undermining evidence-based decisions.

To do more faster, cyber investigators are adopting AI and large language models (LLMs), not realizing that these systems lack requisite knowledge. Without the expertise in planning an investigation, circumventing known problems, evaluating digital evidence, and conveying forensic results, increased speed raises the risk of unseen errors. Applied carelessly, AI is an amplifier, accelerating our existing flaws while adding new ones. Applied responsibly, AI can solve persistent challenges and ensure epistemic security in cyber investigations.

Epistemic security protects cyber investigations against procedural, technical, and cognitive vulnerabilities, as well as wrong or misleading information.

Epistemic Blindness in Cyber Investigations

Epistemic blindness in cyber investigations stems from procedural, technical, or cognitive pitfalls that prevent us from recognizing or resolving crucial gaps in our knowledge. A concrete example is when tool output is treated as factual, but it actually involves uncertainty.

Other sources of epistemic blindness in cyber investigations include:

  • Cognitive bias that causes mistakes and misinterpretations;
  • Cyber investigation procedures that skip important steps;
  • Missing important evidence because of undetected data tampering; and
  • Reasoning errors that cause incorrect conclusions.

The open source, ontology-backed SOLVE-IT knowledge base that I co-develop helps mitigate a wide range of potential weaknesses in cyber investigations.

AI Amplification of Epistemic Blindness

Epistemic blindness is amplified when individuals performing cyber investigations lack the necessary expertise and defer to AI. In general, LLMs are not trained on validated cyber investigation materials and do not provide the correct and optimal specialized knowledge for the situation. This can lead to cyber investigation practices and forensic techniques not being performed properly, and associated weaknesses can be blind spots in the AI that the users may never see. The users do not know how to find and fix gaps in the AI, and the AI is not aware of its own gaps. The latest update to the SOLVE-IT knowledge base catalogs ways that epistemic blindness arises when using an AI-based prompt for interrogating digital evidence, and provides mitigations.

Tampering Exacerbates Epistemic Blindness

Another source of epistemic blindness in cyber investigations is when data has been concealed, altered, or destroyed. Failing to detect tampering and taking available data as authentic can miss relevant digital evidence. When investigating well-resourced groups or AI agents that can execute rigorous manipulation methods, it is important to look for staging and misdirection.

Cyber attacks perpetrated by AI, particularly the recent incidents involving frontier models hacking external systems during testing, include data tampering to conceal actions and avoid detection. Investigating AI-driven cyber attacks requires specialized digital forensics knowledge and techniques to ensure that the outcome is complete and accurate. Cyber investigations that use AI without mitigations for epistemic blindness may be more efficient but are prone to mistakes, missed opportunities, and misinterpretations.

Epistemic Security in Cyber Investigations

Given the growing domain complexity and knowledge gaps, there is a pressing need for systematic and efficient approaches to codifying and reusing existing cyber investigation expertise to ensure accurate and reliable forensic findings. AI will be part of cyber investigations from now on, both as a tool and subject. The critical decision is to use AI in ways that keep the resulting knowledge trustworthy. This means injecting validated knowledge where AI is likely to introduce or amplify epistemic blindness, giving people and AI agents access to expertise they need to eliminate those blind spots. Mentoring professionals and teaching students throughout my career, I have used the following approaches to ensuring epistemic security:

  1. Strategic investigative planning: Determine what is required from the investigation and how the objectives can be accomplished most effectively and efficiently.
  2. Error mitigation analysis: Find and fix weaknesses in cyber investigation procedures and tool results, including AI outputs.
  3. Data tampering detection: Screen digital evidence proactively for distinctive signs of data concealment, alteration, and destruction.
  4. Work product scoring: Evaluate cyber investigation reports and other work products to detect and address deficiencies in structure, clarity, reasoning, and standardization.

Each of these approaches can be bolstered using AI that is grounded in validated structured knowledge to improve the reliability of results and reduce errors, omissions, delays, waste, rework, and cost.

Eoghan Casey is Chief Knowledge Officer at Cyber Knowledge Engineering, is on the Board of Directors of DFRWS.org, and is an internationally recognized expert in cyber investigation, digital forensics, and incident response.

item.title: AI Puts Relevance in Context
item.dc:creator: Esther Shein
item.description: LLMs based on publicly available data have limited effectiveness without the context of a specific industrial or enterprise setting.
item.content:encoded:
You wouldn’t provide personal details to someone, even a friend, out of the blue. Statements need context. In the same way, context is becoming a fundamental mandate for AI as it moves from providing productivity gains to autonomous decision making in the enterprise.

Because context shapes how the AI understands and generates outputs, AI agents need to understand what people mean—not just what they say. Large language models (LLMs) are based on publicly available data, limiting their effectiveness in industrial and enterprise contexts. Yet industry experts say applying context in LLMs is not easy.

“Without context, AI is blind,” said Martin Nevický, an enterprise data architect at Prague, Czech Republic-based data enterprise platform provider Dawiso. “Most of what a model is doing is predicting the next token based on the context of the entire world it was trained on,” he said. “Feed it the right information about your business, and the answer gets dramatically more precise and grounded; instead of a good guess, you get something close to a fact.”

That translates to more reliable answers, fewer hallucinations, and far greater confidence in how the model reaches business decisions, Nevický said.

“For most companies, the key stumbling blocks for enterprise-wide AI adoption are internal silos and the need to embed AI into your operating model,” wrote Bernhard Schaffrik, a principal analyst at Forrester, in a recent blog post. “This requires a deep understanding of how you operate. Process intelligence data can provide exactly this understanding.”

When paired with GenAI, process intelligence data provides the context that AI needs to deliver reliable, relevant, and repeatable outcomes that are aligned with an operating model, Schaffrik said.

While today’s enterprises operate through people performing specialized roles, “Tomorrow’s enterprises will increasingly rely on AI agents to augment and automate those same roles,” observed Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis, which has developed a process intelligence/context model. To succeed, those agents need more than general intelligence, Shah said. They need the operational knowledge required to perform enterprise tasks within a specific business.

This is critical because current frontier AI models “are extraordinary reasoning generalists,” Shah added. “An AI model may know what an invoice is or how a supply chain works in theory, but it doesn’t know a company’s unique approval rules, operational dependencies, or why one exception makes sense while another doesn’t.”

If AI isn’t given that operational understanding, it is forced to make educated guesses based on generic patterns rather than a specific business reality. “And guessing is costly for an enterprise,” Shah said.

Nevický said “LLMs are still a black box to us; nobody can say with certainty how a model will respond to a given input.” In certain vertical industries such as banking and insurance, that makes them virtually useless. “A context layer is what lets us hand the model the right facts to work from, instead of leaving it to guess.”

The missing ingredient isn’t more intelligence; it is context, Shah said. “When AI is grounded in a real-time understanding of how a business operates, it can reason correctly, act reliably, and ultimately be trusted to support and automate enterprise roles rather than simply generate recommendations.”

AI models predict based on patterns, and in the case of LLMs, the patterns are the ones they’ve learned from the public Internet, according to a recent Celonis blog post on the topic of context.

“AI models don’t know about how your specific invoices are related to your shipping records because that data is proprietary, private, and fragmented across internal systems, applications, and devices,” according to the post. “And without that deterministic foundation—the ground truth of your operational reality—no AI agent can be trusted to make reliable real-time decisions and take actions that effectively drive your business outcomes.”

Applying context is not a simple proposition; it depends on a variety of factors including the situation, as well as language, culture, and region. Enterprise operations can only get this context from process data, business knowledge, and real-world observations and experiments.

Schaffrik said he has seen huge success among companies that have adopted proprietary large- and mid-sized language modules. The relevance of outcomes is much higher than among other companies that have adopted publicly available AI systems, Schaffrik said. “Trust levels, therefore, are higher.”

When LLMs are embedded with context, it reduces—but does not eliminate—the risk levels of them hallucinating, Schaffrik added. “What neither well-trained LLMs nor context can fully avoid is that these large language models, to some extent, hallucinate and do things you don’t want them to do, and that’s because the way they are designed doesn’t make them fully repeatable.” That is the difference between the so-called deterministic technologies that are based on logic like one plus one equals two, or if you do this, then do that; that can be encoded in language models that are based on “similarity searches.” That means when someone asks something of a huge LLM, the model looks for similar sentences with a similar frequency of words—it looks for patterns, Schaffrik said.

“The closer they are getting with those patterns, they just spit them out,” Schaffrik said. “Because they don’t understand what they do, they don’t have a consciousness, so similarity search is a good thing, but it only gets you very close to what you’re looking for by accident, and neither context nor well-trained models can avoid that.”

Perhaps a bigger concern is that context can also be used by hackers for nefarious purposes, such as automating cyberattacks. A new technique known as “context bombing” exploits the fact that LLMs are inherently vulnerable to prompt injection, when they are manipulated by deceptive text to ignore their original instructions and safety guidelines and leak sensitive data.

Yet even with documentation, having a context layer doesn’t make a model safe by default; it just changes what can go wrong, Nevický noted. “AI often doesn’t even need to hallucinate to cause real damage; it’s enough that it surfaces a real piece of information that was simply catalogued in the wrong place.”

For example, Nevický pointed to a bank with an internal AI assistant that branch staff rely on when they’re unsure of something. “The bank serves both retail and corporate clients—ask about a retail client, and if corporate-segment rules quietly bleed into the answer, the guidance is built on entirely the wrong foundation,” Nevický said. “That has real consequences.”

Now push that to a client-facing chatbot, which is where the industry is heading. “If your data isn’t well-mapped, sensitive information can end up exposed in that context by accident; information that should never have gotten out at all,” he said. “In a heavily regulated industry, with real money and real people’s data on the line, that’s not a minor slip. It’s a regulatory, reputational, and legal problem.”

Nevický also pointed to the fact that definitions drift, systems change, and stale context can mislead an agent just as badly as no context at all, so someone has to keep checking that meaning indefinitely, not just set it up once and walk away. “And it only works if people actually take the time to document what they know; if that job falls only to the technical team, you capture the plumbing and miss the business knowledge that mattered most,” Nevický said.

None of this is a reason to skip applying context to models, he added. “It’s simply the price of not turning an agent loose on raw, unchecked data.”

While AI is unlocking new capabilities, infusing AI with context must be approached the right way, Nevický said. “More often than not, the slower, steadier path turns out to be the correct one, especially once regulation, real money, and client trust are all on the line,” he said. “Get the context right, and the model stops guessing and starts reasoning from what’s actually true about your business, which is exactly where we started.”

Esther Shein is a freelance technology and business writer based in the Boston area.

item.title: Programmable Money
item.dc:creator: Sriram Ramakrishnan
item.description: Cross-border payments break most assumptions about transactional consistency, network reliability, and state synchronization.
item.content:encoded:
A few years back, I was reviewing the treasury operations of a mid-sized marketplace that sold into eight countries. Strong product, loyal users, but the engineering team spent a third of their sprint cycles on something that should have been invisible: fragile scripts to determine which virtual ledger received which incoming wire, reconciling references truncated in transit, chasing correspondent fees that arrived as unexplained deductions, and manually constructing batch payout CSV files for global sellers every Friday afternoon.

None of that was a business problem; it was a distributed systems plumbing problem. Cross-border payments break almost every assumption we make about transactional consistency, network reliability, and state synchronization. Two decades building this infrastructure has made that clear in ways no architecture diagram communicates.

The Two Flows That Run Everything

Every platform that manages digital commerce relies on two foundational pipelines:

Collections: Architecting how money enters your platform: identifying who sent it, in what currency, via which local clearing rail, and ensuring that inbound funds map deterministically to a specific ledger or transaction.

Disbursements: Managing how money leaves: paying out to sellers, contractors, or suppliers globally, handling localized currency rails, and guaranteeing that the funds reached the intended destination with full confirmation.

In a domestic context, both flows are abstracted away by reliable national clearinghouses. Cross-border breaks that abstraction. When a buyer in Germany pays a merchant in Jakarta, the payment traverses a correspondent chain where reference fields get truncated, fees are deducted mid-flight, and settlement arrives days later looking nothing like the outbound instruction.8,9 Platforms absorbed this operationally for years—reconciliation headcount, manual exception queues, write-offs. A generation of programmatic infrastructure has reframed the problem: the bank account as a programmable object.

Programmable Account Infrastructure: What the Market Looks Like

Global accounts are no longer static relationships managed through banking portals. They are API-provisioned objects—created at scale, bound to specific users or transactions, wrapped in compliance logic, managed in code. Four providers illustrate how different architectural bets produce different outcomes:

Wise Platform: Wise turns its global network into an embeddable utility. A partner calls the API to provision multi-currency virtual accounts for merchants or freelancers—each with native local routing: a U.K. sort code, a eurozone IBAN, a U.S. routing number.10 Each merchant gets a dedicated isolated endpoint, so inbound funds arrive pre-attributed. The account architecture resolves attribution before money moves, structurally eliminating an entire class of reconciliation work.

Airwallex: Airwallex focuses on APAC corridors and platform monetization depth. Its Global Accounts product supports collections across 70-plus countries with payouts to 120-plus.3 The differentiator is how it treats embedded finance as a configurable revenue layer: FX markup capture, fee splits, and card issuance pipelines as composable configuration. By August 2024, Airwallex had surpassed $100 billion in annualized transaction volume, up 73% year-on-year.2

Payoneer: Payoneer brings 20 years of marketplace payout depth through integrations with Amazon, Upwork, Airbnb, and Fiverr.5 Full-year 2024 results reported total volume of $80 billion,6 up 21% year-on-year. Its technical moat is what it does with that data: sitting in the merchant receivables stream lets it underwrite working capital against real-time sales signals.7 The disbursement pipeline becomes a credit engine.

Currencycloud (Visa): Currencycloud operates as a wholesale infrastructure layer,4 providing virtual account and FX APIs that fintechs, neobanks, and regulated institutions embed into their own products—typically white-labeled, invisible to end users. It is the connective tissue between local clearing rails and modern application stacks, built for institutions that need regulatory coverage without constructing the infrastructure themselves.

The account has become programmable. That shifts reconciliation from an operational problem solved by headcount into an architectural property solved at design time.

Where Each Approach Has Limits

The choices among these providers are architectural, not cosmetic:

The Engineering Problems That Remain

No provider abstracts away the distributed systems complexity that emerges when software meets asynchronous payment networks at scale. Two problems land on every team regardless of infrastructure choice.

Deterministic Exception Handling and Idempotency

Payment rails fail in non-deterministic ways. An API call may return 202 Accepted and the underlying network may fail hours later—a downed correspondent node, a compliance freeze, a currency restriction that did not exist at initiation. If a webhook arrives out of sequence or fails to deliver, your system must resolve the state ambiguity without double-crediting a balance or silently dropping a transaction. Building idempotent state machines across every branching failure mode is unglamorous, necessary engineering. None of the providers in this post do it for you.

Distributed Currency Risk Between Collection and Disbursement

A platform collecting in EUR and disbursing in MYR carries FX exposure in the window between receipt and payout. Multi-currency balances let you defer forced conversion, but the logic for deciding when to convert, at what threshold, and how to hedge sits entirely above any provider. Teams that treat payment rails as asynchronous state systems with real failure modes—not reliable remote procedure calls—build platforms that hold up when the correspondent chain breaks, the webhook fires twice, or the reference field arrives empty. That understanding comes from working through the failures.

Disclosure: The observations, product characterizations, and arguments in this post draw on my own professional experience evaluating and building cross-border payment infrastructure. I used AI writing tools for light editing and phrasing assistance during revision. All substantive content, architectural assessments, and the overarching argument originated with me. I reviewed every sentence and take full responsibility for its accuracy.

2. Airwallex. Airwallex Processing Volume Surges Past $100 Billion, Business Wire (15 August 2024), accessed June 2026; https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20240815996981/en/Airwallex-Processing-Volume-Surges-Past-$100-Billion

3. Airwallex. Global Accounts: Local Collections and Payouts Infrastructure. Airwallex Developer Docs (2025), accessed June 2026; https://www.airwallex.com/uk/global-accounts

4. Currencycloud (Visa). International Payment Solutions and Infrastructure: Collect, Convert, Pay (2024), accessed June 2026; https://www.currencycloud.com/solutions/

Sriram Ramakrishnan writes about digital finance, payments infrastructure, and embedded finance. He is a product leader with more than two decades of experience building cross-border payment systems across Asia, Europe, and the Middle East.

item.title: We DO Know How, but Not the How We Want
item.dc:creator: Robin K. Hill
item.description: We know exactly how an LLM works. It's a computer program.
item.content:encoded:
There are so many things about computing that are interesting . . . which we miss while bogged down in AI muck. Among the many misnomers, misstatements, and anthropomorphized mischaracterizations, we find this: We don’t even know how generative AI works! This misleading wave toward the ineffable appears regularly in the popular press. For a recent occurrence, we read, in an article by Peter Denning: “[large language models] are ‘black boxes,’ meaning we have no idea what is going on inside. When we look inside, we cannot make sense of what we see—a huge neural network with millions of nodes and billions of weighted connections. The network gives no clue why it delivered an output, or how to correct it if an output is in error.”1 Okay, some of these statements come from venerable experts, and we know what they mean. But others don’t.

This literal claim of ignorance is absurd. We know exactly how it works. It’s a computer program. We just don’t have any readily accessible account in the surface-level terms that we would like. Machine learning just draws a line from input to output. That line does not pass through the set of holistic features, identifiable attributes, and causal relationships we want to use.

We know how payroll computation works: the program multiplies hours times pay rate. We could do that by hand! We know how address search works: the program compares the query to each database entry until it matches, then outputs the address field. But when we see a chatbot producing the word “delve” after the phrase “for greater understanding, we should,” we go all giddy. Yet we understand these things: Parsing into tokens and probability assignments in real numbers is followed by cycles of matrix multiplication, subtraction, sorting, and more arithmetic, involving incorporation of vast contexts that adjust the magnitude of elements’ effects. Based on the huge corpora sampled, the word ‘delve” follows the given string of tokens with high probability. We could do that by hand! (Given the span of a lifetime, only in theory, which is still significant.) In other words, the achievement in reasoning is quantitative, not qualitative.

When we go to a casino (not that we do), we see the croupier spin the roulette wheel one way and toss the ball the other way, where it goes around and around, until the deflectors slow it down enough so that it settles into a pocket. The only giddiness suffered by the players is based on their bets, winning or losing. No one says, “We just don’t know how it works!” as if that selection of a pocket were some sort of emergent miracle. And we could determine the outcome of the roulette spin to the level of deterministic explanation had we but world enough and time, extensive time, and all the relevant physical formulas at our fingertips. Even without that, we still “know how it works.” One might challenge the analogy thus: the roulette wheel does not provide an answer to a question, just a final outcome . . . but that’s exactly what a chatbot does.

Even plain old statistics produces results that may surprise us, but we don’t claim ignorance about how statistics works: The mean, median, and mode are the results of counting, sorting, adding, and dividing a whole lot of numbers. Didn’t we learn this way (without full biological explanation) that smoking causes cancer? We can validate and interpret a statistical result if necessary by following all the (possibly voluminous) calculations that demonstrate it. We understand that plain old statistics also draws a line from input to output without passing through interpretation.

An article in The New York Times Magazine explores worries about this opaque aspect of diagnostic and recommender systems, and describes new approaches to producing explanation and interpretation.2 That is an admirable endeavor, and, importantly, it is an endeavor predicated on knowing exactly how AI models work. Interpretability is a good goal, but it remains a distortion to call the lack of a gloss, in the terms we want, an impenetrable mystery.

The amazing thing is not that LLM application has escaped epistemic bounds, or achieved magic, or something like that, but that our collective discourse is so incredibly well modeled by token prediction based on context. What to make of that? Like the physics underlying the roulette wheel, the juicy part is not the observation, but the science of the phenomenon. We would be better served by investigating that, by seeking the theory that guides the generation of natural language, than marveling at the lack of casual, causal, intentional, interpretation that we want.

References

1. Denning, P.J. The Conundrum of LLMs. Communications 69:3 (2026), 31-34.

2. Whang, O. A Mind of Its Own. The New York Times Magazine (April 26, 2026).

Robin K. Hill is a lecturer in the Department of Computer Science, an adjunct in the School of Computing, and an affiliate of the Department of Philosophy and Religious Studies, at the University of Wyoming. She has been a member of ACM since 1978.
